attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click the palette to select a background image for this project?
steps.instructions:
Use JavaScript to add a background image to this project! 


Open Scene, drag out [set background image to (img)] into the editor, next to the number 1. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 


scene.setBackgroundImage(img`...`)

In JavaScript, the names of things like functions and variables appear in camelCase because there cannot be spaces between words. Instead, a capital letter is used to indicate where there would normally be a space between multiple words.


After the JavaScript text appears on the editor, click the palette to the left of the line of code, then choose a background image from the Gallery.


Click ▶ to see the background image appear in the project.

steps.hints: ❓Did you rename the sprite using camelCase?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about the way the let mySprite = sprites.create(img`...`, SpriteKind.Player) JavaScript code is formatted? How is it similar and different to setting a sprite in blocks?

❓ What kind of name describes the sprite image chosen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide the ninja in dragging the code block into the JavaScript editor, so that it appears on the correct line. They can drag the block to the end of the first chunk of code, so that it appears directly below it.

💡Help the ninja highlight all of mySprite and point out the importance of formatting and syntax; the dot, let, and equal sign should not be deleted and the ninja should use camelCase in their sprite name. Just as in blocks, sprite names should not have spaces.
steps.instructions:
Add a sprite to this project! 


Open Sprites, drag out [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] onto a blank line under the existing code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

let mySprite = sprites.create(img`...`, SpriteKind.Player)

In the JavaScript editor, certain keywords will appear in the color blue. The word let appears in blue to indicate that a new variable is being defined.


After the JavaScript text appears, click the palette to select a sprite. In the editor, highlight mySprite and replace it by typing a new sprite name using camelCase. Give the sprite a simple name that describes what it is, such as myCat.


Click ▶ to see the sprite appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you type the sprite’s name in mySprite.setPosition(x, y), and update the x and y parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja: 

❓ Where might the sprite appear on the screen?

❓ Why should a sprite’s position code be placed after the code that sets the sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:  

💡 Explain to the ninja the difference between a parameter and an argument. Parameters are the names listed in the function definition (e.g. x-coordinate parameter). Arguments are the actual values inside the parentheses that are passed to the function (e.g. (0,0)).

💡 Point out to the ninja that the visual coordinate grid does not exist in the JavaScript editor to help them map out where to place a sprite. Remind the ninja that the x coordinate value range is 0-160, and the y coordinate value range is 0-120.

💡 Larger x values move the sprite to the right, and smaller x values move the sprite left. Larger y values move the sprite down, smaller y values move the sprite up.
steps.instructions:
Set the sprite in a different position!


Open Sprites, drag out [set (mySprite) position to x y] onto a blank line under the existing code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

mySprite.setPosition(0, 0)

In the editor, highlight mySprite and replace it with the sprite name from the previous step. Type the sprite name exactly the same, otherwise the code will not run correctly.


There are 2 arguments that send information to the setPosition function. Inside the parentheses, replace the first argument (0) with a number between 0 and 160 for the x position, and replace the second argument (0) with a number between 0 and 120 for the y position. 


In the JavaScript editor, numbers will appear in the color green. The x and y parameters appear in green because they are passing a number argument to the function.


Click ▶ to see the sprite appear in a different position.

steps.hints: ❓Did you type the sprite’s name and update the string inside the quotation marks in mySprite.sayText(text)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What would happen if the quotation marks were deleted in the mySprite.sayText(“:)”) code?

❓ What might the sprite say when it appears on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Arguments can also be string values. Remind the ninja that arguments are the values inside the parentheses that pass information to the function.

💡 Point out to the ninja that instead of using a drop down menu or having parameters already set like in blocks, they must type them out in JavaScript. Make sure the ninja has replaced mySprite with the name of their sprite and they have included a new string within the quotation marks. 

💡Explain to the ninja that syntax is critical when working in JavaScript text. The quotation marks in the mySprite.sayText(“:)”) code tell the project that the parameter has a string value.
steps.instructions:
Make the sprite say something! 


Open Sprites, drag out [(this) say (:))] onto a blank line under the existing code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

mySprite.sayText(“:)”)

In the editor, highlight mySprite and replace it with the sprite’s name. Highlight the argument :) inside the quotation marks, and replace the text with something for the sprite to say, such as “hello world!” 


In the JavaScript editor, strings appear inside quotation marks in the color red. The quotation marks must surround the entire string for the code to work.


Click ▶ to see the sprite say something!

steps.hints: ❓Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Does the code work as expected in blocks?

❓ What do you think might be easier about coding in blocks? What do you think might be easier about coding in JavaScript?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja make connections between the JavaScript text they have just written and their background knowledge of using blocks. Ninjas should be very familiar with these blocks and concepts already, so encourage them to think about what they think is easier or harder about coding in text instead of blocks.
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Look over the syntax of the code in this project: the capitalization of certain letters, the spacing, and the symbols - commas, parentheses, and quotation marks. Notice that changing the syntax might make the project unable to run. 


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks!  Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how are sprite names and other parameters formatted in blocks, compared to JavaScript?

subgroups.title: Hello World!
subgroups.introduction: Create your first project in JavaScript! Set a background image, add 1 sprite, position it on screen, then make it say something!

validationItems.text: Use 1 sprite with a custom name.
Set the position of the sprite.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll move from using blocks to code to using JavaScript, and learn about JavaScript code and syntax! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: And Now For Something New
badges.description: Use the MakeCode JavaScript editor to add sprites and set their properties.

badges.title: Opening Line
badges.description: Write your first line of JavaScript code.

badges.title: Coordinating Coordinates
badges.description: Set a sprite’s position in JavaScript.

badges.title: String Theory
badges.description: Add a string to a function’s parameter in JavaScript.

badges.title: Palette Cleanser
badges.description: Use a number to set the background color of a scene in JavaScript.

badges.title: Truth Hurts
badges.description: Use a Boolean value to set a sprite’s property in JavaScript.

badges.title: Gaining a Following
badges.description: Set a sprite to follow another sprite in JavaScript.
